O.outcome_detail: Self-reported reduction in tension during operation

cells.quote: A significant number also noted that virtual reality technology helped alleviate anxiety during procedures (59/61, 96.72%)
cells.note: This was a descriptive questionnaire of DVRS participants only; the study provides no comparison condition or inferential test against a baseline.

O.outcome_detail: Self-reported improvement in clinical operational skills

cells.quote: A significant number also noted that virtual reality technology helped alleviate anxiety during procedures (59/61, 96.72%) and honed their clinical operational skills (57/61, 93.44%).
cells.note: The operational-skills finding is self-reported and descriptive; no non-DVRS comparison group or pre-post test was reported.

O.outcome_detail: Self-reported interest in learning and confidence entering clinical practice

cells.quote: Additionally, the technology was credited for boosting their enthusiasm for learning and confidence in clinical practice (58/61, 95.08%).
cells.note: This was a descriptive DVRS-group questionnaire; the study did not compare confidence or interest with traditional-manikin students.

D.treatment: desktop VE-based simulation with visual and auditory interaction

O.outcome_detail: perceived multisensory immersion, attractiveness, and enjoyment of repeated practice

cells.quote: Almost all participants reported that the D-VSim not only provided visual perception, but also stimulated auditory sensation, which was consistent with previous research [44]. They also perceived that the D-VSim made repeated activity more immersive and attractive, which could not be achieved with previous traditional training.
cells.note: Qualitative interview perceptions; no quantitative effect size or controlled comparison was reported.

O.outcome_detail: understanding and following ADL skill-training procedures

cells.quote: The textual description of skill training is lengthy and obscure, particularly when expressed with a cluster of jargon. Fortunately, I can understand the meaning of each paragraph and follow the steps of each activity by using the D-VSim system. It truly saves a great deal of time and effort. [P9]
cells.note: Participants perceived the simulation as improving understanding relative to conventional PowerPoint learning; no objective learning measure was reported.

O.outcome_detail: interest, enjoyment, and initiative to learn

cells.quote:
Some participants were surprised that “the time is passing so fast when I am studying” [P8], which suggested that they may have achieved a state of flow.

Some participants said that “I take the initiative to open the system for learning, and this behavior or phenomenon has never happened before indeed” [P7].
cells.note: The study reports participants' perceptions of increased engagement and initiative, not a controlled comparison of motivation.

D.treatment: desktop VE-based simulation with repeatable practice

O.outcome_detail: willingness to continue studying and repeat activities

cells.quote: It is much fun using the virtual simulation for learning as it changes the original way of thinking that learning is a tedious process. Like game-playing, this virtual simulation learning can evoke similar feelings. Therefore, I can study for longer periods without feeling like giving up. [P6]
cells.note: This is a participant-reported perception of persistence; the quoted claim is not an experimentally measured duration or completion outcome.

cells.quote: The virtual simulation should be used as an auxiliary learning tool. The conventional PowerPoint learning can build the foundation of knowledge acquisition, while the virtual simulation can cement it for reinforcement. To be precise, virtual simulation is better functional as a post-class rather than an in-class learning strategy. [P12]
cells.note: This is a participant perception from a qualitative interview, describing virtual simulation as complementary reinforcement rather than a replacement for PowerPoint learning.

D.treatment: Internet-accessible desktop virtual simulation on personal devices

O.outcome_detail: perceived accessibility and flexible stopping and resuming of learning

cells.quote: Participants also reported that they preferred virtual simulation for learning because of its accessibility and repeatable practice opportunities. As one participant explained, “it gives me maximal opportunities to learn…I can use the iPad and login into the system anytime and anywhere, such as library, canteen, and café” [P5]. Once the Internet is connected to my device, such as iPad, I can access to the system. It is much easier to operate and control the system. If I have to handle other businesses, I can stop it and resume when available. [P16]
cells.note: Qualitative participant perceptions; the study does not report a quantitative effect size.

D.treatment: desktop VE-based simulation with integrated multimedia resources

O.outcome_detail: Understanding and following ADL skill-training procedures

cells.quote:
Participants believed that virtual simulation separated the whole skill training process into its small-piece individual components and made it more understandable and straightforward. Examples demonstrated “how virtual simulation can simplify rehabilitation process for stroke patients, such as completing upper body dressing activities or transitioning from a supine to a side-lying position for patients with hemiplegia” [P4].
